analysis.title: GS Sector Specialists: Energy, Natural Resources and Utilities Preview Sentiment Check + Two Stocks (5 Nov 2026)
key_insights: Refining: specialists agree the medium-term outlook on cracks screens most bullish versus oil or gas. Near-term revisions are the issue: bears cite a rolling gasoline crack, less confidence in diesel crack upside, and possible de-escalation abroad. The author says the starting point should be the crude differential, not products.
Merchant refiners are about 20% off their October highs. Questions center on building cash versus leaning into buybacks with stocks off their peaks.

Oil: a lot of the risk premium has come out of the barrel over the last couple of trading sessions. Oil E&P is well owned by the dedicated community, and the open question is how much more length leaves the group.

Desk conversations show a clear preference for International-linked oil equities over the Permian. Higher capex (service cost inflation, steel, diesel) was one of the main talking points this EPS season.

Gas: the one area of O&G where macro views have not shifted. The strip looks challenging, Permian growth and its associated gas volumes are top of mind, and feedback on the international gas trade is 'this is played out'. There has been more 'hiding in gas' given uncertainty on oil and products. The incremental buyer is specialists, and generalists are largely not involved (unchanged).

IPPs: no real sense yet of playing defense or offense. Specialists have been neutral for some time and there is no valuation discussion because there is no conviction on the floor or FCF yield to step in. Generalist inbounds are more cautious, which the author reads as telling about length in the group.
PJM versus ERCOT has been the IPP trade over recent weeks, with more willingness to lean into PJM given uncertainty on when (if) demand shows up in Texas.

BTM (behind-the-meter power): the most asked question yesterday was whether BTM holds up even with the TX/OH updates. The author expects focus today on dispersion between Tier 1 and Tier 2 players, based on contracts, cash flow, signed equipment and financing needs. The bull pitch is that contracts are at or near the finish line into year-end, and slippage is the largest risk power investors flagged.

Solar: debate over whether the recent price action is real demand or short covering. The author makes the case that after the midterms outcome the space was due for a bounce given light positioning and negative skew on expected near-term guidance downgrades, calling it a 'coiled spring'. Inbounds are more on utility scale than residential.

SEI fell 17% on 4 Nov. The author found the size of the move perplexing, since the quarter had a strong EBITDA beat above the high end of guidance and raised 4Q26 and 1Q27 guidance. Total capacity under long-term contracts is now 3.2 GW with an 11-year average tenor, and the 15-year agreement was highlighted again. The author prefers Tier 1 operators and says SEI fits.

COP reported EPS on the morning of 5 Nov: EPS ahead of the Street, production largely in line, CFO ahead. 4Q guidance is a little softer than expected and is likely to be picked at. Capex update showed no change to FY guidance, with early 2027 thoughts likely to be asked on the call.

COP is one of the more well-owned E&P stocks, with a desk positioning score of 9/10, one of the highest for Conoco in some time. Willow progress (first oil early 2029) and the formulaic returns approach were well received. The author expects positioning to drive the day's trading but sees more holders willing to defend the story.

market_movers.rationale: The author says there is a preference to own Tier 1 power operators and SEI fits. The 17% drop followed a strong EBITDA beat above guidance's high end and raised 4Q26 and 1Q27 guidance.

EPS ahead of the Street with CFO ahead and unchanged FY capex guidance. 4Q guidance is softer, and positioning at 9/10 will drive the trading reaction, though more holders are willing to defend the story.
